evidence.claim: Mountain roads connect conifer forests with the palms of the desert
evidence.quote: From clusters of desert palms to high country conifer forests and snow-capped mountains

evidence.claim: Palms to Pines links Banning Pass and Palm Desert across 67 miles of mountain and desert country.
evidence.quote: This 67-mile route will take you from Palm Desert past snow-peaked mountains to Banning Pass.

evidence.claim: The Forest Service emphasizes the contrast between desert palms and high-country conifer forests along this National Forest Scenic Byway.
evidence.quote: From clusters of desert palms to high country conifer forests and snow-capped mountains, experience a contrast of ecosystems within a short distance.

evidence.claim: Its Banning section offers views toward the San Gorgonio Wilderness; Highway 243 is a two-lane road with curves and switchbacks.
evidence.quote: San Gorgonio Wilderness area to the north on the Banning Pass section of the byway.

evidence.claim: The Banning-to-Idyllwild road was under construction in 1904 and completed as an oiled road in September 1910.
evidence.quote: A road from Banning to Idyllwild was under construction in 1904

evidence.claim: The federal government contributed $2,000 because the road was expected to help haul lumber and fight fires.
evidence.quote: it was expected to help with transporting lumber and stopping fires; because of this, the federal government provided $2,000 for the construction.

evidence.claim: Riverside County supervisors named the mountain-to-desert highway Palms to Pines in 1930.
evidence.quote: On August 11, 1930, the Riverside County Board of Supervisors officially named the highway "from San Jacinto Mountains to the Desert" as the Palms to Pines Highway.

evidence.claim: The Banning road joined the state highway system as Route 243 in 1970.
evidence.quote: SR 243 was added to the state highway system in 1970.

evidence.claim: From Banning, take Highway 243 up the switchbacks and through forest to Pine Cove and Idyllwild, then continue to Mountain Center.
evidence.quote: The highway traverses north along a winding road through the community of Idyllwild. SR 243 makes a left turn at the intersection with Circle Drive and continues through Pine Cove. The road continues through the forest past Mount San Jacinto State Park through Twin Pines and the Morongo Indian Reservation before making a few switchbacks and descending en route to the city of Banning

evidence.claim: Highway 74 follows Garner Valley, crosses the Santa Rosa Indian Reservation and passes Pinyon Pines.
evidence.quote: SR 74 follows the Garner Valley Wash through Garner Valley before meeting the eastern terminus of SR 371. The road crosses the Santa Rosa Indian Reservation before going through the communities of Ribbonwood and Pinyon Pines

evidence.claim: It turns along Deep Canyon and descends beside Carrizo Creek into Palm Desert.
evidence.quote:
turning north along Deep Canyon and becoming the western boundary of the University of California Desert Research Area.
As the highway descends to the Coachella Valley area, it parallels Carrizo Creek before entering the city limits of Palm Desert

evidence.claim: National Forest Scenic Byway
evidence.quote: The Palms to Pines Scenic Byway is a National Forest Scenic Byway.

evidence.claim: Highway 243 is a two-lane road with curves and switchbacks.
evidence.quote: State Route 243 (SR 243) is a 30-mile (48-kilometer) two-lane state highway

evidence.claim: completed as an oiled road in September 1910.
evidence.quote: The oiled road was completed by September 1910

evidence.claim: then continue to Mountain Center.
evidence.quote: runs from SR 74 in Mountain Center to Interstate 10 (I-10) in Banning.

evidence.claim: Strawberry Creek runs year-round through the high mountain valley occupied by Idyllwild.
evidence.quote: Idyllwild lies mostly within a high mountain valley bisected by a small year-round stream, Strawberry Creek.

evidence.claim: The town was first known as Strawberry Valley, after the wild fruit growing beside the creek.
evidence.quote: Idyllwild was originally known as Strawberry Valley because of the wild strawberries that grow there, especially beside the creek

evidence.claim: A toll road from Hemet opened the area to logging and tourism by the 1890s.
evidence.quote: By the 1890s a toll road had been built from Hemet, which opened Idyllwild to settlement, logging, and tourism.

evidence.claim: Automobiles later made it a weekend destination for Southern Californians.
evidence.quote: With the advent of the automobile, Idyllwild became a weekend tourist attraction for Southern Californians.

evidence.claim: For years, businesses adopted German-sounding names to present an alpine village, a practice that ended during World War II.
evidence.quote: For many years, the town presented itself as an alpine village, and hotels and businesses had German or German-sounding names, but this practice ended during World War II.

evidence.claim: Tahquitz Peak and Suicide Rock flank the town.
evidence.quote: Idyllwild is flanked by two large rock formations, Tahquitz Peak  and Suicide Rock

evidence.claim: Pinyon Pines takes its name from the native pinyon pines in this small valley between the San Jacinto and Santa Rosa mountains.
evidence.quote: It is located in a small valley between the San Jacinto Mountains and Santa Rosa Mountains, north of State Route 74. It takes its name from the Pinyon pine (Pinus monophylla) trees native to the area.

evidence.claim: The community sits north of Highway 74 at approximately 4,000 feet.
evidence.quote: Pinyon Pines sits at an elevation of approximately 4000 feet.

evidence.claim: Its beginnings are tied to roadbuilding: Art Nightingale founded it in the 1930s, around the time the Pines to Palms Highway was being built.
evidence.quote: Pinyon Pines was founded by Art Nightingale in the 1930s, around the time that the Pines to Palms Highway was being constructed.

evidence.claim: A mechanic who invested in Pinyon Flats, Nightingale built accommodations for highway workers and the Sugarloaf Cafe, which has since closed.
evidence.quote: A mechanic by trade, he invested in the Pinyon Flats area. He built accommodations for the workers of the highway, and also built the Sugarloaf Cafe, now since closed.

evidence.claim: Seven Level Hill, a stretch of Highway 74 just south of Palm Desert, supplied the opening encounter in the 1963 comedy It's a Mad, Mad, Mad, Mad World.
evidence.quote: A segment of Route 74 named "Seven Level Hill," just south of Palm Desert, California, appears in the 1963 American comedy film It's A Mad, Mad, Mad, Mad World during the opening minutes of the film

evidence.claim: The principal characters meet here after a car accident near mile marker 87.
evidence.quote: when the major characters of the film meet for the first time following a car accident (near mile marker 87).

evidence.claim: Along the Banning Pass section, the view also takes in craggy mountains and the developed valley floor below.
evidence.quote: Admire fantastic views of the urbanized valley floor below, craggy mountains, and the San Gorgonio Wilderness area to the north on the Banning Pass section of the byway.

evidence.claim: The road became part of the forest highway system in 1927, before its later state designation.
evidence.quote: The road became a part of the forest highway system in 1927.

evidence.claim: A sanatorium built in 1901 to treat tuberculosis patients was soon remodeled as a resort.
evidence.quote: In 1901, the Idyllwild Sanatorium was built to treat tuberculosis patients. It was soon remodeled as a resort
